title: The Yajnavalkya Smriti
author: yajnavalkya
attributionNote: Ascribed to the Vedic sage Yajnavalkya; the text was compiled centuries after him and carries the rules of the schools rather than the speech of the sage.
description: The Yajnavalkya Smriti sets out dharma in three books: conduct — study, the sacraments, marriage, gifts and the duties of the stages of life; the rules of a state, of procedure and of evidence, and of the sale of goods, pledges and servants; and expiation. Its second book is the most systematic treatment of law in the older smritis and became the working law of much of India through the commentary upon it.
historicalContext: Where the Laws of Manu are the smriti quoted most often, the Yajnavalkya Smriti is the one used most often in court, because it states the rules more clearly and in a better order. In Bengal it was read with the Mitaksara and in northern India with the Balakrida, and the British Indian courts took it — with those commentaries — as the Hindu law they were bound to apply.
availabilityNote: Complete: all three kandas, 1,011 verses of the GRETIL e-text, streamed at read time one kanda at a time. This is the Sanskrit text; no English translation is imported here.
